To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the collapse of Soviet hierarchies can be explained by the combination of decentralizing reforms and a breakdown of central authority, which in turn resulted from the inability of the center to enforce its reputation as an arbiter of disputes; and that (2) in China, the center’s ability to enforce its reputation for punishing transgressions, combined with the rise of hybrid forms of ownership, made it difficult for local agents to appropriate organizational assets.

the collapse of centrally administered organizations in the Soviet Union was caused by a loss of central control over local agents, whereas the persistence of such organizations in China was due to the preservation of such control.

1) Soviet and Chinese reforms transferred significant autonomy from central to local agents; 2) Soviet reforms led to the breakdown of central hierarchies, while Chinese reforms did not; and 3) the key difference between the Soviet and Chinese experiences was that the Chinese center preserved its reputation for discipling local agents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a central problem of the postcommunist transition, and more broadly with the problem of the collapse of centrally administered organizations.
the conditions under which hierarchies break down and with the role of central authority in preserving hierarchies.
the breakdown of authority and the disintegration of organizations under conditions of ambiguous ownership rights, and with the factors that can prevent such disintegration from occurring.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Soviet system was a failure, and China’s system was a success.
the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is a very powerful institution that has survived the transition from communism to capitalism and has been strengthened by the process.

China has been able to avoid collapse of its state hierarchies by maintaining a credible threat to use coercion to punish agents for opportunism, and by creating a system of property rights that allows the center to retain control of the most valuable assets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Soviet Union was a state that collapsed from within, whereas China was a state that survived a crisis of legitimacy.
the Soviet Union was a state in which the central authorities lost control over their own state, while China was a state in the process of building its own state.
the neoinstitutional approach provides a useful framework for understanding the disintegration of Soviet organizations and the relative success of the Chinese reforms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Soviet Union’s collapse can be explained as an organizational failure of the center to preserve the reputation of central authorities, while the persistence of central political and administrative institutions in China can be explained in large part by the center’s success in maintaining its reputation for monitoring and sanctioning.
the breakdown of centrally planned organizations is a function of the interaction between the institutional context and the incentives facing agents within hierarchies.
the central state in China retained the ability to discipline local agents, and this capacity was a critical factor in the preservation of state and Party authority.
